title: AP Investigation: ICE Body Camera Policy Allows Director to Withhold Footage from Fatal Shootings
excerpt: An Associated Press investigation revealed that ICE's body camera policy—adopted in February 2025—allows the agency director to withhold or indefinitely delay release of footage from fatal shootings and serious injuries when doing so is deemed in the 'best interests of the agency.' ICE simultaneously announced a full camera rollout by end of August 2026.
content:
On August 7–8, 2026, the Associated Press published an investigation into ICE's body-worn camera policy, finding that the agency's own rules—adopted in February 2025—give the ICE Director broad discretion to withhold footage from the public following fatal shootings and other serious use-of-force incidents.

The policy states that footage from incidents involving serious bodily injury or death in custody should be released within 72 hours "if in the best interests of the agency," but further allows the director to "withhold or indefinitely delay the release" if there are "specific and compelling circumstances" that redaction cannot resolve. Critics noted that this effectively gave ICE unilateral control over public accountability for its most consequential encounters.

  • ICE Acting Director David J. Venturella simultaneously announced that the agency was "on track to equip every officer and agent in the field with body-worn cameras by the end of August"—a $30.9 million Axon contract that, according to former ICE chief of staff Jason Houser, began one day after the July 13 Maine fatal shooting, making it "clearly a political response."
  • Congress had appropriated $20 million for ICE cameras on April 30, 2026, following the January Minneapolis shootings. ICE had received $75 billion in the 2025 budget but purchased no cameras from that appropriation.
  • CBP had similarly declined to release body camera footage from the fatal January 2026 shooting of Alex Pretti in Minneapolis, telling lawmakers it would be made public "when it's appropriate."
  • Sociology professor Christopher Schneider noted: "In some ways, ICE is saying the quiet part out loud."
